final_proof:
**Conventions.** $X$ is a $1$-manifold (possibly with boundary). As usual this means a Hausdorff space in which every point has an open neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open subset of $\mathbb R$ or of $H=[0,\infty)$. (Hausdorffness is really needed. In the line with three origins $0_1,0_2,0_3$, take $L=(-1,0)\cup\{0_1\}\cup(0,1)$. Its closure also contains $0_2,0_3,-1,1$, which is four points.) By hypothesis there is a diffeomorphism $I\to L$ from an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$. All we use is that it gives a continuous injective map $I\to X$ with image $L$. If $I=\varnothing$ then $L=\varnothing$ and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise compose with a homeomorphism $(0,1)\to I$ (e.g. an affine map, or $\tan$/$\log$-type maps for unbounded $I$). This gives a **continuous injective** $f:(0,1)\to X$ with $f((0,1))=L$.

Define the two *end sets*
$$E_1=\bigcap_{0<c<1}\operatorname{cl} f((c,1)),\qquad E_0=\bigcap_{0<c<1}\operatorname{cl} f((0,c)).$$

**Step 1: $\operatorname{cl}L\setminus L\subseteq E_0\cup E_1$.**
Take $0<c<1/2$. Then $L=f((0,c))\cup f([c,1-c])\cup f((1-c,1))$. The set $f([c,1-c])$ is a continuous image of a compact set, so it is compact, and therefore closed in the Hausdorff space $X$. The closure of a finite union is the union of the closures, so
$$\operatorname{cl}L=\operatorname{cl}f((0,c))\cup f([c,1-c])\cup\operatorname{cl}f((1-c,1)).$$
Let $p\in\operatorname{cl}L\setminus L$. Then $p\notin f([c,1-c])\subseteq L$, so $p\in \operatorname{cl}f((0,c))\cup\operatorname{cl}f((1-c,1))$ for every $c\in(0,1/2)$.
Suppose $p\notin E_0$ and $p\notin E_1$. Then there are $c_0,c_1\in(0,1)$ with $p\notin\operatorname{cl}f((0,c_0))$ and $p\notin\operatorname{cl}f((c_1,1))$. Let $c=\min(c_0,1-c_1,1/4)\in(0,1/2)$. Then $(0,c)\subseteq(0,c_0)$ and $(1-c,1)\subseteq(c_1,1)$. Hence $p\notin\operatorname{cl}f((0,c))$ and $p\notin\operatorname{cl}f((1-c,1))$, which is a contradiction. So $p\in E_0\cup E_1$.

**Step 2: $E_1\setminus L$ has at most one point.**
Suppose $p\neq q$ both lie in $E_1\setminus L$. Since $X$ is Hausdorff, there are disjoint open sets $U_0\ni p$ and $V\ni q$.

*Choice of a chart interval.* Let $\psi:W\to\psi(W)$ be a chart at $p$, where $\psi(W)$ is open in $\mathbb R$ or in $H$. The set $\psi(W\cap U_0)$ is an open neighbourhood of $\psi(p)$ in $\mathbb R$ or in $H$, so it contains a set $K$ of one of two kinds:
- (a) an open interval $(\psi(p)-\varepsilon,\psi(p)+\varepsilon)$;
- (b) a half-open interval $[0,\varepsilon)$, which is needed only when $\psi(p)=0\in\partial H$.

Put $U=\psi^{-1}(K)$. This is open in $X$, contains $p$ and does not meet $V$. Compose $\psi|_U$ with an affine map. This gives a homeomorphism $\varphi:U\to J$ where either (a) $J=(-1,1)$ with $\varphi(p)=0$, or (b) $J=[0,1)$.

*A fact used below.* A continuous injective real function $g$ on an open interval $(\alpha,\beta)$ is strictly monotone; this follows from the intermediate value theorem. So its one-sided limits $\ell_\alpha=\lim_{t\to\alpha^+}g$ and $\ell_\beta=\lim_{t\to\beta^-}g$ exist in $[-\infty,\infty]$ and are distinct. The image $g((\alpha,\beta))$ is exactly the open interval between them.

Let $T=f^{-1}(U)$. It is open in $(0,1)$, so it is a disjoint union of open intervals, its components.

*Claim A.* Let $(\alpha,\beta)$ be a component of $T$ with $\beta<1$. Then $\lim_{t\to\beta^-}\varphi(f(t))$ exists and lies in $\overline J\setminus J$, where $\overline J$ is the closure in $\mathbb R$. The same holds at $\alpha$ if $\alpha>0$.
*Proof.* The map $g=\varphi\circ f$ is continuous and injective on $(\alpha,\beta)$, so it is strictly monotone with values in the bounded set $J$. Hence the limit $y$ exists and $y\in\overline J$. Suppose $y\in J$. Since $\varphi^{-1}$ is continuous, $f(t)=\varphi^{-1}(g(t))\to\varphi^{-1}(y)\in U$ as $t\to\beta^-$. But $f$ is continuous at $\beta\in(0,1)$, so $f(t)\to f(\beta)$. Limits are unique in a Hausdorff space, so $f(\beta)=\varphi^{-1}(y)\in U$. That means $\beta\in T$, which contradicts $\beta$ being an endpoint of a component of the open set $T$. The case of $\alpha$ is the same. $\square$

*Claim B.* Every component $(\alpha,\beta)$ of $T$ has $\alpha=0$ or $\beta=1$.
*Proof.* Suppose $0<\alpha<\beta<1$ and let $g=\varphi\circ f$ on $(\alpha,\beta)$. By Claim A, $\ell_\alpha,\ell_\beta\in\overline J\setminus J$, and these limits are distinct.
- In case (b), $\overline J\setminus J=\{1\}$, so $\ell_\alpha=\ell_\beta=1$. This is impossible.
- In case (a), $\overline J\setminus J=\{-1,1\}$, so $\{\ell_\alpha,\ell_\beta\}=\{-1,1\}$. Then $g((\alpha,\beta))=(-1,1)\ni 0$, so $p=\varphi^{-1}(0)\in f((\alpha,\beta))\subseteq L$. This contradicts $p\notin L$. $\square$

*Conclusion of Step 2.* Components are disjoint, so at most one component of $T$ has the form $(0,\beta)$. Fix any $c\in(0,1)$.
- Since $p\in\operatorname{cl}f((c,1))$ and $U$ is a neighbourhood of $p$, there is $t>c$ with $f(t)\in U$, i.e. $t\in T$.
- Since $q\in\operatorname{cl}f((t,1))$ and $V$ is a neighbourhood of $q$, there is $s>t$ with $f(s)\in V$. Then $f(s)\notin U$, so $s\notin T$.

So the component of $T$ containing $t$ is $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\beta\le s<1$. By Claim B, $\alpha=0$, so it is the unique component of the form $(0,\beta^*)$, and $\beta^*>t>c$. Since $c\in(0,1)$ was arbitrary, $\beta^*=1$. Then $T\supseteq(0,1)$, i.e. $L\subseteq U$. But the point $f(s)\in L$ found above lies in $V$, which is disjoint from $U$. This is a contradiction. Hence $E_1\setminus L$ has at most one point.

**Step 3: $E_0\setminus L$ has at most one point.** Apply Step 2 to the continuous injective map $\tilde f(t)=f(1-t)$. It has the same image $L$, and its set $E_1$ is the $E_0$ of $f$.

**Conclusion.** By Steps 1–3,
$$\operatorname{cl}L\setminus L\subseteq(E_0\setminus L)\cup(E_1\setminus L),$$
and this is a union of two sets with at most one point each. Therefore $\operatorname{cl}L$ contains at most two points not in $L$. $\blacksquare$
